reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AABB Technical Manual
clinicalPearls: Commonly defined as replacement of roughly one whole blood volume within about 24 hours, or transfusion of around ten or more red cell units in that period; rapid-loss definitions (several units within an hour) are also used in trauma
Modern resuscitation favours a balanced ratio of red cells, plasma, and platelets that approximates whole blood rather than red cells alone, to limit dilutional coagulopathy
The lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy compounds bleeding and must be actively prevented with warmed fluids and blood products
Citrate anticoagulant in stored products binds calcium, so ionised hypocalcaemia is common during rapid transfusion and should be monitored and corrected
Hyperkalaemia can occur, especially with older stored red cells and rapid infusion in neonates or patients with renal impairment
Point-of-care viscoelastic testing (thromboelastography or ROTEM) helps guide targeted product replacement in preference to fixed ratios once bleeding is controlled
Tranexamic acid given early in traumatic haemorrhage reduces mortality; early activation of an institutional protocol streamlines product delivery
reference.pathophysiology: Massive haemorrhage and its replacement produce a combination of dilutional and consumptive coagulopathy: clotting factors and platelets are lost with bleeding and diluted by crystalloid and red cell replacement. Hypoperfusion drives metabolic acidosis and, together with infusion of cold products, causes hypothermia; both impair enzymatic clotting and platelet function. Citrate load from banked products chelates ionised calcium and magnesium, further impairing coagulation and cardiac contractility, while potassium leaked from stored red cells can accumulate. The result is a self-perpetuating cycle of bleeding, impaired haemostasis, and shock unless actively interrupted.
additionalDifferentials: Surgical or mechanical bleeding requiring intervention
additionalInvestigations: Serial full blood count, prothrombin time/INR, activated partial thromboplastin time, and fibrinogen
Ionised calcium, potassium, and arterial blood gas with lactate and pH
Viscoelastic haemostatic assays (TEG/ROTEM) for goal-directed replacement
Type and crossmatch with repeat sampling to detect ongoing loss
redFlags: Ongoing uncontrolled haemorrhage with haemodynamic instability requiring emergency surgical or interventional haemostasis
Refractory hypocalcaemia with cardiovascular compromise during rapid transfusion
Persistent coagulopathy despite balanced product resuscitation, suggesting DIC or hyperfibrinolysis
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends chiefly on control of the bleeding source and speed of resuscitation; early balanced transfusion, prevention of the lethal triad, and timely antifibrinolytic therapy improve survival, whereas delayed correction of coagulopathy and shock markedly increases mortality.
pitfalls: Over-reliance on crystalloid resuscitation, worsening dilutional coagulopathy and tissue oedema
Neglecting patient and fluid warming, allowing hypothermia-driven coagulopathy
Forgetting to monitor and replace ionised calcium during rapid citrate exposure
Continuing fixed high-ratio product delivery after bleeding is controlled rather than switching to laboratory-guided replacement
management: Activate a major haemorrhage protocol with early, balanced transfusion of red cells, plasma and platelets approximating whole blood
Achieve rapid definitive control of the bleeding source by surgical, endoscopic or interventional radiology means
Give an antifibrinolytic (tranexamic acid) early, particularly in trauma
Prevent and correct the lethal triad by warming the patient and all fluids and products and by correcting metabolic acidosis
Monitor and correct citrate-induced ionised hypocalcaemia with intravenous calcium
Monitor for and treat hyperkalaemia, especially with rapidly infused older red cell units
Transition to viscoelastic-guided (TEG/ROTEM) goal-directed component replacement once bleeding is controlled, with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate for hypofibrinogenaemia
Involve transfusion, haematology and critical care teams
